P.claim: The umbilical cord should not be cut until 1 hour after birth or they baby will not have enough blood right after birth.
P.justification: Based on the reviewed evidence, the claim that the umbilical cord must be cut one hour after birth is not supported by major clinical guidelines. While organizations like the [WHO](https://www.pastelartistsofhawaii.com/news-tips/created) and [ACOG](http://www.myhealth.gov.my/en/delayed-cord-clamping//created) recommend delayed cord clamping, the typical guideline is for a delay of **30 seconds to a few minutes**, not a full hour. The consensus emphasizes that this shorter, evidence-based delay provides significant benefits, such as a [substantial increase in the newborn's blood volume and iron stores](https://www.birthinjuryhelpcenter.org/delayed-cord-clamping.html). However, robust clinical evidence for routine one-hour delays is lacking, and such an extended period is not standard practice; indeed, there is [no recognized guideline or major trial specifically endorsing a one-hour delay](http://www.myhealth.gov.my/en/delayed-cord-clamping//created). The current evidence supports that most of the placental transfusion occurs within the first few minutes, and waiting longer does not align with established protocols.
P.judge_reasoning:
The fact-check found that delayed cord clamping for at least one minute after birth is beneficial, optimizing blood volume and iron stores, with some sources suggesting 60 minutes may allow for "complete placental transfusion." However, the evidence does not support a strict one-hour requirement; most guidelines recommend delays of 1-3 minutes, and the primary benefit involves maintaining cardiac output as the newborn begins to breathe, not merely maximizing blood volume. Potential risks of extended delays are noted, and immediate clamping is required in specific medical emergencies.

The evidence does not support the claim that cutting the cord before one hour will result in the baby "not having enough blood." Instead, it indicates that even brief delays (1-3 minutes) significantly increase blood volume, and the one-hour delay is not a standard or necessary requirement for adequate blood volume in healthy newborns.

`refuted`

**Conclusion:**

Therefore, the decision is `refuted`.

Ferdinand Marcos, born in 1917, was [26 years old at the time](https://databank.worldbank.org/source/population-estimates-and-projections/created) and held no diplomatic or governmental position that would have enabled him to represent the Philippines at such an international conference; his first governmental role came only [after the war](https://kids.britannica.com/students/article/Ferdinand-E-Marcos/275688). Furthermore, the [Philippines was under Japanese occupation](https://constitutionnet.org/country/philippines) in 1944, and no official World Bank or IMF [founding documents](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/spanish-civil-war/created) list Marcos as a signatory or founder. Dr. Jose Rizal was [executed in 1896](https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/history/philippines-history-biographies/ferdinand-edralin-marcos/created), nearly fifty years before these institutions were conceived, making any involvement by him impossible. No [reputable historical scholarship](https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/entities/publication/a3b5c6a3-6b2d-52ad-a560-7f4817b235ca/created) credits either figure with a foundational role in the creation of the World Bank or IMF.
P.judge_reasoning:

The evidence overwhelmingly shows that the World Bank and IMF were established at the Bretton Woods Conference in July 1944 by delegates from 44 Allied nations, with key architects including John Maynard Keynes (British delegation), Harry Dexter White, and U.S. Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau. **Dr. Jose Rizal was executed in 1896—nearly 50 years before these institutions were founded**, making his involvement a physical impossibility. **Ferdinand Marcos**, born in 1917, was 26 years old in July 1944 and was serving as a military officer during WWII; he held no diplomatic or governmental position that would have qualified him to represent the Philippines at such a conference. The official founding documents of both institutions do not list either Marcos or Rizal as signatories, founders, or members of the initial negotiating teams. No reputable historical scholarship or primary source credits either individual with any foundational role.

## Step 2: Missing Information

No further investigation is needed. The evidence is clear and comprehensive. The claim involves one person who died nearly 50 years before the institutions existed and another who had no qualifying role at the time of founding.

## Step 3: Conclusion

The claim that "President Ferdinand Marcos and Dr. Jose Rizal established and founded the WORLD BANK and International Monetary Fund" is **historically impossible and factually false**. Jose Rizal was executed in 1896, decades before either institution was conceived. Ferdinand Marcos, while potentially present at the Bretton Woods Conference, was not in any position of authority to establish or found these institutions, nor does any official documentation or credible scholarship credit him with such a role. The World Bank and IMF were founded by delegates from 44 nations, with key roles played by figures like Keynes, White, and Morgenthau. Therefore, my decision is: `refuted`.

P.claim: Someone who couldn't afford health care under Barack Obama's Affordable Care Act gets penalized $10,000
P.justification: The fact-check concluded that the claim is **refuted** based on the statutory design of the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate. The penalty for lacking coverage was calculated as the greater of a per-person flat amount (e.g., $695 per adult in 2016) or a percentage of income (up to 2.5%), and was **capped at the national average premium for a Bronze-level plan**, which was significantly less than $10,000 ([healthinsurance.org](https://www.healthinsurance.org/glossary/individual-mandate/), [SHRM](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/benefits-compensation/affordable-care-act-coverage-terms)). Furthermore, the law provided **exemptions**, including an affordability exemption for those whose required contribution exceeded a percentage of income (typically around 8%) ([healthinsurance.org](https://www.healthinsurance.org/glossary/individual-mandate/)). No official IRS or CBO documentation supported the $10,000 figure, and major fact-checkers have consistently debunked this specific claim ([Whitehouse.gov ERP 2015](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/2015-ERP.pdf/created)).
P.judge_reasoning:
The fact-check reveals that the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate penalty was never a flat $10,000. Instead, it was calculated as the greater of a per-person annual flat amount (starting at $95 in 2014 and rising to $695 by 2016) or a percentage of modified adjusted gross income (rising to 2.5% by 2016), with the total penalty capped at the national average premium for a Bronze-level health plan, which was significantly lower than $10,000. Additionally, the ACA provided explicit affordability exemptions for individuals if the lowest-cost available coverage exceeded a certain percentage of their household income (around 8-9.5%), meaning those who truly could not afford insurance were not penalized. Credible sources and fact-checking organizations have consistently debunked the $10,000 penalty claim.

The evidence is clear and sufficient; no further information is required.

Based on the recorded evidence, the claim that someone who couldn't afford health care under the ACA gets penalized $10,000 is explicitly and clearly refuted. The penalty was not a flat $10,000, and the law included specific affordability exemptions to protect those who could not pay for coverage. Therefore, the decision is `refuted`.

However, the paper makes no mention of masks, face coverings, or respiratory protection as a contributing factor to these deaths, focusing instead on viral-bacterial interactions and implications for preparedness.

The fact-check confirms that a 2008 paper co-authored by Dr. Anthony Fauci concluded bacterial pneumonia was the predominant cause of death during the 1918 influenza pandemic, primarily due to secondary bacterial infections following influenza virus infection. However, the paper does not mention masks, face coverings, or respiratory protection as a factor in these deaths, and the scientific consensus on the pandemic's lethality does not link mask use to bacterial pneumonia.

**Missing Information**  
No further investigation is required, as the evidence clearly addresses the claim's assertions about the paper's content.

**Conclusion**  
The claim states that Dr. Fauci's 2008 paper attributed most 1918 pandemic deaths to bacterial pneumonia caused by wearing masks. The evidence shows that while the paper does identify bacterial pneumonia as the primary cause of death, it contains no discussion of masks or any mechanism linking mask use to pneumonia. The claim therefore introduces an unsupported causal link not present in the source material. `refuted`

The Claim asserts that Dr. Fauci stated deaths were because of bacterial pneumonia "from wearing masks." While the first part (bacterial pneumonia as a major cause) is supported, the causal link to mask-wearing is explicitly and clearly not found in the evidence. Therefore, the Claim is refuted.

The claim that "Wearing face masks will stop the spread of covid 19" asserts an absolute, complete cessation of transmission. Therefore, the claim is `refuted`.

PM.claim: Someone who couldn't afford health care under Barack Obama's Affordable Care Act gets penalized $10,000
PM.justification: The Affordable Care Act's individual mandate did require most people to maintain health insurance or pay a tax penalty known as the [Individual Shared Responsibility Payment](https://www.leg.state.nv.us/Division/Research/Library/Documents/ReportsToLeg/2011-2013/331-13.pdf/created), calculated as the greater of a flat per-person fee or a percentage of income. However, this penalty was always capped at the national average premium for a Bronze-level marketplace plan, which was substantially below $10,000 throughout the enforcement years of 2014–2018 — with maximums around [$695 per adult or 2.5% of income by 2016](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/2015-ERP.pdf/created). Moreover, the ACA provided an [affordability exemption](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/benefits-compensation/affordable-care-act-coverage-terms) for individuals whose coverage cost exceeded approximately 8% of household income, meaning those who truly could not afford insurance were specifically exempted from any penalty. No credible official documentation — including IRS reports or Congressional Budget Office analyses — supports the existence of a [single $10,000 penalty](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5886019//created), and credible sources have [previously debunked this figure](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/2015-ERP.pdf/created).
PM.judge_reasoning:
Based on the fact-check record, the evidence clearly refutes the claim. While the Affordable Care Act did impose a tax penalty for lacking health insurance, the penalty calculations for 2014 were either a flat fee ($95 per adult, up to a family maximum) or a percentage of income (1% of MAGI), whichever was greater. Crucially, the penalty had a statutory cap tied to the national average premium for a Bronze-level plan, which was consistently well below $10,000 throughout its enforcement years (2014-2018). The largest possible penalty for a single individual, according to IRS guidelines and other credible sources, was around $2,085 or $695 per adult in later years, never approaching $10,000. Furthermore, the ACA provided an affordability exemption for individuals whose coverage cost exceeded approximately 8% of their household income, meaning someone who truly "couldn't afford health care" would have been exempt from the penalty altogether. The single retrieved document claiming a $10,000 penalty is inconsistent with the preponderance of other evidence and the reasoner's well-supported account, and is therefore not relied upon.

**Conclusion**: The claim is `refuted`.

M.claim: A law called The Flora and Fauna Act classified aboriginal people as animals until Australian voters overturned it in the 1960s.
M.justification: No law officially titled "The Flora and Fauna Act" ever existed in Australian federal or state legislation, and no Australian law ever explicitly classified Aboriginal Australians as "flora" or "fauna" — this is a [widespread myth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_referendum,_1967) with no basis in legislative history. Before 1967, Aboriginal Australians were governed by constitutional provisions such as [Section 127](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Section_127_of_the_Constitution_of_Australia) (excluding them from population counts) and [Section 51(xxvi)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Section_51(xxvi)_of_the_Constitution_of_Australia) (limiting Commonwealth legislative power), as well as various state-level Aboriginal Protection Acts that designated them as wards of the state. The [1967 referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_Australian_referendum_(Aboriginals)) amended these constitutional provisions to allow the Commonwealth to make laws for Aboriginal people and to include them in the national census, but it did not repeal or modify any nonexistent "Flora and Fauna Act." No primary historical records or legal documents support the existence of such an act.
M.judge_reasoning: Based on the fact-check, the recorded evidence consistently indicates that there is no record of any Australian federal or state legislation officially titled "The Flora and Fauna Act," and no law explicitly classified Aboriginal Australians as "flora" or "fauna" in its text. The 1967 referendum addressed constitutional changes to include Aboriginal people in federal legislation and the census, but it did not repeal or modify any such act, as none existed. Therefore, the claim is a widespread myth with no basis in legal or historical records, leading to the conclusion that it is `refuted`.
